check-what-a-polymorphic-type-promises.title: Check: what a polymorphic type promises

questions.question: A function has type `[a] -> Bool`. Which of the following behaviours could it actually have?
options: Return True exactly when the list is empty
Return True exactly when every element is equal to the first
Return True exactly when the largest element is positive
Return True exactly when the list contains the number 7
questions.explanation: Checking for emptiness only requires pattern matching on [] versus (x:xs) — a purely structural check that needs no operation on the elements at all. The other three all inspect and compare or add the elements, which an unconstrained a forbids.
optionFeedback: Correct — this only asks 'is the list []', a structural question the type variable a is never involved in answering.
Comparing elements to one another requires ==, which needs an Eq constraint the signature does not have.
Deciding 'largest' needs comparison (Ord), and 'positive' needs a numeric type (Num or Ord); [a] -> Bool has neither.
Checking for a specific element like 7 requires == against a concrete numeric literal, which again needs Eq and Num — not available for an arbitrary a.

questions.question: Why must `pick x y = x` (type `a -> b -> a`) return x rather than something built from y?
options: Haskell's syntax forbids referring to y in the body
a and b are required to be the same type, so y already has type a
Nothing about type b is known, so no terminating computation on y could ever produce a value of type a
pick is only allowed to use pattern matching, not its arguments directly
questions.explanation: b is a completely independent, unconstrained type variable. Since the result must have type a, and the only value of type a available is x itself, nothing you could terminatingly do with y — of the arbitrary, unrelated type b — could produce that result.
optionFeedback: Haskell's syntax is not the limitation here; you could write y in the body (e.g. as an unused binding). The limitation is what a well-typed, terminating result can be built from.
They are independent variables and may differ — pick 5 'z' above instantiates a to Integer and b to Char, which are not the same type.
Correct — with no constraint on b, there is no operation available to turn a b-typed value into an a-typed one, so only x itself can be the answer.
pick uses no pattern matching at all in this definition; the restriction comes from typing, not from which syntactic forms are legal.

questions.question: In `map show [1,2,3]`, what does GHC instantiate map's two type variables to?
options: a := Integer, b := Integer
a := Integer, b := String
a := String, b := Integer
It cannot be determined without a type annotation
questions.explanation: map :: (a -> b) -> [a] -> [b]. The list [1,2,3] fixes a to Integer, and show :: Show a => a -> String fixes b to String — matching :type map show reported as [a] -> [String] with a still Show-constrained.
optionFeedback: b cannot be Integer: show's result type is always String, whatever its argument type is.
Correct — the list argument fixes a to Integer, and show's result type fixes b to String, giving map show :: Show a => [a] -> [String].
a is fixed by the list [1,2,3], not by show's result; this has the two the wrong way round.
It is fully determined here: the list supplies a and show's return type supplies b, with no ambiguity.

questions.question: `headOf [True, False]` and `headOf "cat"` both call the same `headOf :: [a] -> a`. What does this demonstrate?
options: headOf is secretly two different functions chosen by overloading
a is instantiated independently to Bool for one call and to Char for the other, with no relationship between them
a must be the same type in every call to headOf, so one of these calls is actually rejected
headOf secretly requires an Eq constraint to run
questions.explanation: Instantiation happens per call. Nothing links the a chosen for headOf [True, False] to the a chosen for headOf "cat" — they are two entirely separate applications of the same one definition.
optionFeedback: There is exactly one headOf, one piece of compiled code; overloading (Chapter 9's next lesson) is a different mechanism from parametric polymorphism.
Correct — each application of headOf instantiates a on its own; two different calls may pick two entirely different, unrelated types.
The 'one type per application' rule (Section 3) applies within a single call, where a variable appears more than once — it says nothing about two separate calls needing to agree.
headOf's definition, (x:_) = x, uses no operation on the element at all, so it needs no constraint whatsoever.

questions.question: Why can `countLeaves :: Tree a -> Int` be fully polymorphic while `sumTree` needs `Num a =>`?
options: countLeaves is shorter to write
countLeaves never examines the values stored in the tree, only its Leaf/Branch structure; sumTree applies + to those values, which requires Num
Tree a only permits numeric elements when summed, never when counted
sumTree is recursive and countLeaves is not
questions.explanation: countLeaves pattern matches on the constructors alone and adds 1 or recurses — the values inside Leaf are never touched, so a needs no operations. sumTree extracts those values and adds them with +, which exists only for Num instances.
optionFeedback: Line count has nothing to do with which constraints a signature needs; it is entirely about which operations the body actually uses on a-typed values.
Correct — this is exactly the reasoning from Section 2 applied to a recursive data type: no operation on a means no constraint needed.
Tree a places no restriction on a in the data declaration itself; the restriction, if any, comes only from what a particular function does with the values.
Both functions recurse, one equation per constructor; recursion is not what distinguishes their constraints.

questions.question: Why is `Pair` alone, with no type arguments, not a type?
options: Pair is a reserved keyword in Haskell
Pair is a type constructor: like Tree, it needs its type arguments supplied (Pair Int String) before it denotes an actual type
Pair can only ever hold two values of the same type
Pair needs a type class instance before it becomes a type
questions.explanation: data Pair a b = MkPair a b declares a two-argument type constructor. Exactly as with Tree (one argument) and [] (one argument), a value can only ever have a fully applied type, such as Pair Int String — never the bare constructor.
optionFeedback: Pair is an ordinary name chosen for this lesson, not a language keyword; the reason lies in what a data declaration with type parameters actually creates.
Correct — MkPair a b makes Pair a two-parameter type constructor. A value's type is always the fully applied form, e.g. Pair Int String, never bare Pair.
MkPair a b uses two independent type variables, a and b, precisely so the two fields may differ — as swapPair (MkPair 1 "one") demonstrates.
Instances (Chapter 9's next lesson) govern what operations a type supports; they play no role in whether Pair by itself already denotes a type.
